scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study population is defined as post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) patients with documented occupational SARS-CoV-2 infection and ICD-10 U09.9 diagnosis (Table 1), and the analysis stratifies this PCC cohort by ME/CFS status as a sub-classification within it; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a German cross-sectional study of 92 severely and long-term affected post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) patients, mostly healthcare and social-service workers who had filed for occupational-disease recognition, examined using cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) between July 2023 and March 2025. Nearly half of the cohort met diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS, and the large majority showed objective signs of post-exertional malaise. Most patients showed markedly reduced oxygen uptake and power output on CPET, with about two-thirds meeting the study's objective thresholds for 'absolute work disability,' and these objective measures correlated with self-reported disability (Bell Disability Scale) and with whether patients were on sick leave, in work reintegration, or currently working. The document reports functional/occupational-capacity burden in this specific severe, occupationally-selected cohort; it contains no dollar-denominated medical, non-medical, or indirect cost data of any kind, and no Lyme disease content.

modeled_issues.issue: CPET-based absolute work disability (VO2peak <15 mL/min/kg and/or PPO <1 W/kg)
modeled_issues.population: Severely and long-term affected PCC patients with suspected occupational disease, German healthcare/social-services employees insured by BGW (N=92)
modeled_issues.source_locator: Abstract p.1 ('Overall, 66% of patients met objective thresholds for work disability') and Conclusion p.13 ('Most patients (66.3%) had a VO2peak < 15 mL/min/kg and/or a PPO < 1 W/kg')

contextual_issues: Financial concerns, loan repayments, and job-loss anxiety are mentioned (citing Lemogne & Pitron 2023) as reasons patients continue working despite low physical capacity, but are not measured or quantified within this cohort.
Mental health and cognitive dysfunction are noted as additional factors limiting work ability beyond what CPET captures, but are not quantified in this study.
Health-related quality-of-life impact is referenced via an external citation (Carlile et al. 2024) but is not directly assessed in this cohort.

No mention of caregiver burden, family/household impact, direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), or repeated care-seeking/insurance-access barriers appears anywhere in the document.
evidence_gaps: No dollar-denominated direct medical, direct non-medical, or indirect cost data of any kind are reported anywhere in this document; a cost model would require separate economic data collection not present here.

No data on insurance claims processing, occupational-disease compensation amounts, or outcomes of the BGW recognition process, despite the cohort being recruited specifically through that occupational-insurance pathway.

No general-population PCC/ME/CFS prevalence or cost data originate from this study itself; cited external prevalence figures (e.g., 9.8%–15.4% ME/CFS among PCC) are from other papers, not this study's own measurement, and the document itself attributes its much higher 49% figure to recruitment bias toward severe, occupationally-disabled patients.
No longitudinal follow-up of occupational or financial outcomes after the CPET assessment; data are cross-sectional baseline measurements only from an ongoing telerehabilitation RCT.
No breakdown of any reported burden measure by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool this severe, occupationally-disabled, German healthcare/social-service worker cohort (N=92, 88% female, mean age 50.7, mean symptom duration ~24 months, BGW-insured) with general-population PCC estimates such as the 9.8%–15.4% ME/CFS prevalence cited from other international studies, or with Peter RS et al. (2025)'s population-based cohort reporting VO2peak ~27.9 mL/min/kg two years post-infection — these differ in population selection, severity, and measurement time window.

The RER+ subgroup (patients achieving respiratory exchange ratio ≥1.0, a physiologically validated-effort subset) and the full cohort (N=92) are different population sizes measuring the same CPET variables; percentages reported for each (e.g., 52.9% vs 63% below VO2peak 15 mL/min/kg) must be labeled as subset vs. full-cohort results, not treated as independent comparator estimates.

The document's own stated cohort multimorbidity rate (42%, Discussion) and the external age-matched general-population comparator rate (25.3%, from separately cited studies [46,47]) use different populations and methods (clinical occupational-disability cohort vs. general-population cross-sectional surveys) and should not be pooled as a like-for-like multimorbidity comparison.
No price year or cost figures exist anywhere in this document, so no monetary comparison across time periods or cost perspectives is possible from this source.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: Study inclusion criterion 3 (Table 1) required that each patient's PCC diagnosis be 'established by a family or occupational physician (main diagnosis + ICD-10: U09.9)' before enrollment; all prevalence figures reported for this cohort (e.g., 49% ME/CFS, 66.3% work disability, 79% PEM-positive) are therefore drawn from a population pre-selected on having successfully received that formal ICD-10 diagnosis code, which by the documented access-to-diagnosis mechanism could exclude symptomatic patients who never obtained the code.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: CPET-derived absolute work disability prevalence (66.3%) and the occupational-status distribution (75% sick leave / 12% reintegration / 13% working) are reported as single pooled figures for the whole mixed cohort, stratified only by ME/CFS status and multimorbidity status — not by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, or any other federally tracked subgroup, despite the cohort being 88% female.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a clinical/diagnostic-system gap in which organ-centered, system-specific diagnostics (cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurological) routinely yield unremarkable findings in severely affected PCC/ME/CFS patients and therefore fail to explain or objectively document their work disability, leaving work-ability evaluation reliant on subjective self-report with no established objective diagnostic framework prior to this study's proposed CPET-based approach.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Introduction (p.2): 'Organ-centered clinical diagnostics frequently fail to explain their work disability... isolated, organ or system-specific assessments offer limited insight into global functional impairment,' and Discussion/Conclusion framing CPET as filling this gap for 'individualized therapy planning and return-to-work decisions.'

federal_evidence_used.how_used: Confirms U09.9 is the official ICD-10-CM code for 'Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified,' the same code required by this study's inclusion criteria (Table 1), supporting the claims/diagnosis-code basis cited in claims_undercounting_caveat.

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document would be most useful to occupational-medicine clinicians, disability/insurance evaluators (such as the BGW-type occupational-disease system in this study), and researchers designing PCC/ME/CFS rehabilitation or return-to-work pathways, since the document's core findings link objective CPET thresholds to self-reported disability and current occupational status in a severe, real-world patient population. It cannot inform direct-cost, indirect-cost, or financial-planning questions because no dollar figures are reported anywhere in the source. It is relevant to a narrow, severely affected and occupationally-selected PCC/ME/CFS subgroup, not the general Long COVID population.
use_cases: Occupational-medicine or disability-insurance review: illustrating how objective CPET thresholds (VO2peak <15 mL/min/kg, PPO <1 W/kg) relate to self-reported work status (sick leave vs. reintegration vs. working) within this specific severe, occupationally-disabled PCC cohort, to support (not replace) individualized work-capacity discussions.

Health-related quality-of-life impact is referenced via an external citation (Carlile et al. 2024) but is not directly assessed in this cohort.

No general-population PCC/ME/CFS prevalence or cost data originate from this study itself; cited external prevalence figures (e.g., 9.8%–15.4% ME/CFS among PCC) are from other papers, not this study's own measurement, and the document itself attributes its much higher 49% figure to recruitment bias toward severe, occupationally-disabled patients.
No longitudinal follow-up of occupational or financial outcomes after the CPET assessment; data are cross-sectional baseline measurements only from an ongoing telerehabilitation RCT.
No breakdown of any reported burden measure by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status.

spec.title: Objective Exercise Capacity and Occupational Status in a Severe Post-COVID Condition (PCC) Cohort
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects only a German cross-sectional study of 92 severely and long-term affected post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) patients, mostly healthcare/social-service workers who had filed for occupational-disease recognition and already carried a formal ICD-10 U09.9 diagnosis, assessed by cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) between July 2023 and March 2025. It covers only prevalence-style percentages reported in this specific cohort (objective CPET-based work disability, post-exertional malaise, ME/CFS status, and occupational/sick-leave status). It contains no dollar-denominated cost data of any kind, no general long-COVID population estimates, and no longitudinal or outcome-after-assessment data; none of these figures should be generalized beyond this severe, occupationally-selected, 88%-female sample.

takeaway.patient: In this study of 92 people with severe, long-lasting post-COVID symptoms who had already filed for occupational-disability recognition, exercise testing found objective signs of major physical limitation (very low oxygen uptake and/or muscle power output during exercise) in about two out of three participants. Most also showed objective or reported signs of post-exertional malaise (a worsening of symptoms after physical or mental effort). These objective test results lined up with how disabled people said they felt and with whether they were on sick leave, returning to work gradually, or already working - suggesting that for people like those in this study, 'invisible' exhaustion symptoms can show up on objective testing even when routine organ-by-organ tests look normal.
takeaway.care: In this severe, occupationally-selected PCC cohort, CPET-based objective thresholds for work disability (VO2peak <15 mL/min/kg and/or peak power output <1 W/kg) were met by about two-thirds of patients, nearly half met ME/CFS criteria, and most screened positive for post-exertional malaise. These objective measures correlated with self-reported disability (Bell Disability Scale) and with actual occupational status (sick leave vs. reintegration vs. working), suggesting CPET may usefully complement - not replace - subjective work-capacity assessment in similarly severe patients. The cohort also carried a heavy comorbidity burden (about 91% with at least one pre-existing condition, averaging three per patient), which is clinically relevant to care planning even though a specific ME/CFS-vs-non-ME/CFS multimorbidity difference (67% vs 45%) did not reach statistical significance in this sample.
takeaway.policy: Among 92 severely affected, occupationally-insured PCC patients recruited through a formal ICD-10 U09.9 diagnosis pathway, roughly two-thirds met objective CPET-based work-disability thresholds, and these objective findings tracked with sick-leave, reintegration, and working status. This offers a possible objective complement to self-report within occupational-disability evaluation systems, but the cohort's severe, occupationally-selected, 88%-female composition means these percentages cannot be generalized to the broader long-COVID population, and no cost or cost-effectiveness data exist in this source to support reimbursement or budget decisions.

patient: If you experience unexplained crashes in energy or function after physical or mental effort, you could ask your care team whether objective exercise testing (like the CPET used in this study) might help document your limitations - and ask about the risks of symptom flare-ups from the test itself before agreeing to it.

Keep in mind this study focused on a severe, mostly female, already-diagnosed group of healthcare and social-service workers who had filed occupational-disability claims; ask your own provider how closely your situation matches this group before assuming these percentages apply to you.

If you are pursuing a disability or occupational-insurance claim, you could ask whether objective exercise-capacity findings, alongside your own reported symptoms, can be part of what's considered in your evaluation.
care: Consider screening for post-exertional malaise (e.g., with a validated questionnaire) before ordering cardiopulmonary exercise testing, since it was common in this severely affected cohort, to weigh the risk of triggering a symptom flare against the diagnostic value of the test.

This finding that objective CPET thresholds tracked with self-reported disability and actual occupational status may be worth checking against your own return-to-work evaluation workflow, as a possible complement to subjective assessment rather than a replacement for it.

Given the high comorbidity load observed here (about 91% with at least one pre-existing condition, averaging three per patient), care coordination across specialties may warrant particular attention for similarly severe PCC/ME/CFS patients.

Note that the apparent difference in multimorbidity between ME/CFS-positive and non-ME/CFS patients (67% vs. 45%) did not reach statistical significance in this sample (p=0.056); avoid treating it as a confirmed group difference in your own protocols.
policy: Consider whether occupational-disease or disability-evaluation frameworks could pilot incorporating objective CPET thresholds alongside self-reported disability scales, given the correlation observed in this severe PCC cohort.

Because this cohort was recruited through successful ICD-10 U09.9 diagnosis and occupational-insurance referral, prevalence figures here (e.g., the 49% ME/CFS rate) likely do not represent the general long-COVID population and should not be used directly for population-level burden or budget projections without further study.

No cost data are reported in this source; commissioning direct and indirect cost data collection within this or a similar occupational cohort would be a prerequisite before this evidence could inform cost-effectiveness or reimbursement decisions.

Since the cohort is 88% female and not disaggregated by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, consider cross-referencing with federal survey data (e.g., MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS), which generally supports such disaggregated analysis, before generalizing these disability prevalence figures across subgroups.

inputs.label: Objective CPET-based work disability rate
inputs.source: Abstract p.1 and Conclusion p.13 ('Most patients (66.3%) had a VO2peak < 15 mL/min/kg and/or a PPO < 1 W/kg'); the 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound covering the full possible percentage, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the 92 studied patients who met the study's objective exercise-test thresholds for work disability; raising or lowering it explores how the downstream comparisons to sick-leave status and occupational engagement would shift under different assumed disability prevalence.

inputs.label: Proportion currently on medical sick leave
inputs.source: p.10 'Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity' (69/92 patients); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the cohort formally on sick leave at assessment; moving it relative to the objective work-disability rate shows how administrative work status and objective exercise-capacity findings do or do not align in this cohort.

inputs.label: Proportion in occupational work reintegration
inputs.source: p.10 'Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity' (11/92 patients); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the cohort in a graduated return-to-work process; it combines with the currently-working share below to show total occupational engagement versus full sick leave.

inputs.label: Proportion currently working
inputs.source: p.10 'Occupational Status in Relation to Functional Capacity' (12/92 patients); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the cohort currently working despite severe PCC; combined with the reintegration share it shows how much of the cohort retains any occupational activity.

inputs.label: ME/CFS prevalence within this PCC cohort
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (45/92 patients meeting Canadian Consensus Criteria); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This shows how common formally diagnosed ME/CFS was within this severe, occupationally-selected PCC subgroup; the document attributes this high figure partly to recruitment bias toward severe cases, not to general PCC prevalence.

inputs.label: Post-exertional malaise (PEM) positive screen rate
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (71/92 patients, DSQ-PEM questionnaire); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This shows how common post-exertional malaise (symptom worsening after exertion) was in this cohort; it contextualizes why exercise-based testing in this population needs careful risk-benefit consideration.

inputs.label: Multimorbidity share among ME/CFS-positive patients
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (30/45 ME/CFS-positive patients with ≥3 comorbidities or ≥1 severe comorbidity); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the comorbidity share within the ME/CFS-positive subgroup; comparing it to the non-ME/CFS subgroup's rate below shows the size of a trend the study itself found did not reach statistical significance (p=0.056).

inputs.label: Multimorbidity share among non-ME/CFS patients
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (21/47 non-ME/CFS patients with ≥3 comorbidities or ≥1 severe comorbidity); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the comorbidity share within the non-ME/CFS subgroup, the comparator for the ME/CFS-positive rate above; the gap between the two did not reach the study's own significance threshold.

outputs.label: Objective CPET-based work disability rate (display)
outputs.interpretation: This restates the share of the 92 patients who met objective exercise-test thresholds for work disability; a higher value means more of this severe, occupationally-selected cohort showed measurable exercise-capacity impairment consistent with inability to work, independent of self-report.

outputs.label: Combined share in work reintegration or currently working
outputs.interpretation: This sums the reintegration and currently-working shares to show the proportion of the cohort retaining some occupational engagement rather than being fully on sick leave; a higher value means more of the cohort kept some work activity despite severe PCC symptoms.

outputs.label: Objective CPET disability rate minus sick-leave rate (positive = more patients meet the objective disability threshold than are formally on sick leave; negative = more patients are on sick leave than meet the objective threshold)
outputs.interpretation: At the document's own baseline values (66.3% objective disability vs. 75% on sick leave), this is negative (about -8.7 percentage points), meaning slightly more patients were on sick leave than strictly met the objective CPET disability threshold in this cohort; it illustrates that formal work status and objective exercise-capacity testing do not map one-to-one here.

outputs.label: Multimorbidity share, ME/CFS-positive minus non-ME/CFS patients (positive = ME/CFS group had a higher multimorbidity share; negative = lower)
outputs.interpretation: At the document's own baseline values (67% vs. 45%), this gap is positive (about 22 percentage points), but the study itself reports this comparison did not reach statistical significance (p=0.056 against its own p<0.05 threshold) and describes it only as 'a trend'; this output should not be read as a confirmed difference between the two groups.

scenarios.label: Pooled multimorbidity (no significant gap)
scenarios.goal: Tests whether the 67%-vs-45% multimorbidity gap survives the study's own non-significant test (p=0.056).
scenarios.description: Sets both ME/CFS-positive and non-ME/CFS multimorbidity rates to the cohort's pooled ~55% rate, reflecting the study's finding that the subgroup difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.056).

scenarios.label: Sick leave matched to CPET threshold
scenarios.goal: Tests whether sick-leave recognition matches objective CPET disability criteria.
scenarios.description: Sets the sick-leave rate equal to the objective CPET-based work disability rate (66.3%), closing the administrative gap the study highlights between subjective sick-leave determination and objective functional testing, illustrative only with no causal mechanism implied.

package.documentation:
## About this simulator

This tool is built from a single German cross-sectional study of 92 severely and long-term affected post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) patients, mostly healthcare and social-service workers who had filed for occupational-disease recognition. All patients had already received a formal ICD-10 U09.9 ('Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified') diagnosis as an inclusion criterion, and were assessed by cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) between July 2023 and March 2025.

### Inputs and outputs
All inputs are percentages the study itself reports for this cohort: the CPET-based objective work-disability rate (66.3%), the proportions on sick leave (75%), in work reintegration (12%), and currently working (13%), ME/CFS prevalence by Canadian Consensus Criteria (49%), post-exertional malaise (PEM) screening positivity (79%), and multimorbidity shares within the ME/CFS-positive (67%) and non-ME/CFS (45%) subgroups. Outputs recombine these into a work-engagement share, a gap between objective disability and sick-leave status, and a multimorbidity gap between the two clinical subgroups. No dollar-denominated costs of any kind are reported anywhere in this source, so no cost or cost-effectiveness output is included.

### Limitations
**Diagnosis-based selection (undercount risk):** because enrollment required an already-established ICD-10 U09.9 diagnosis from a physician, every percentage here describes patients who successfully obtained that code; people with similar symptoms who never received the diagnosis are not captured, so these figures likely do not represent the full burden of post-exertional, functionally limiting PCC in the wider population.

**No subgroup disaggregation:** the pooled work-disability (66.3%) and occupational-status figures are reported only for the whole cohort (and by ME/CFS/multimorbidity status), not broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, despite the cohort being 88% female. Federal survey sources such as MEPS, NHIS, and BRFSS generally support this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this study did not perform it.

**Systemic evidence gap:** the study frames routine organ-centered diagnostics (cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurological) as frequently failing to explain these patients' work disability, leaving work-ability evaluation reliant on subjective report before this CPET-based approach; this is a gap in the diagnostic/evidence system itself, separate from the accuracy of the percentages above.

All figures apply only to this severe, occupationally-selected sample and should not be generalized to the broader long-COVID population.

inputs.label: ME/CFS prevalence within this PCC cohort
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (45/92 patients meeting Canadian Consensus Criteria); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This shows how common formally diagnosed ME/CFS was within this severe, occupationally-selected PCC subgroup; the document attributes this high figure partly to recruitment bias toward severe cases, not to general PCC prevalence.

inputs.label: Post-exertional malaise (PEM) positive screen rate
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (71/92 patients, DSQ-PEM questionnaire); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This shows how common post-exertional malaise (symptom worsening after exertion) was in this cohort; it contextualizes why exercise-based testing in this population needs careful risk-benefit consideration.

inputs.label: Multimorbidity share among ME/CFS-positive patients
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (30/45 ME/CFS-positive patients with ≥3 comorbidities or ≥1 severe comorbidity); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the comorbidity share within the ME/CFS-positive subgroup; comparing it to the non-ME/CFS subgroup's rate below shows the size of a trend the study itself found did not reach statistical significance (p=0.056).

inputs.label: Multimorbidity share among non-ME/CFS patients
inputs.source: p.7 'Clinical Profile' (21/47 non-ME/CFS patients with ≥3 comorbidities or ≥1 severe comorbidity); 0-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the comorbidity share within the non-ME/CFS subgroup, the comparator for the ME/CFS-positive rate above; the gap between the two did not reach the study's own significance threshold.

outputs.label: Objective CPET-based work disability rate (display)
outputs.interpretation: This restates the share of the 92 patients who met objective exercise-test thresholds for work disability; a higher value means more of this severe, occupationally-selected cohort showed measurable exercise-capacity impairment consistent with inability to work, independent of self-report.

outputs.label: Combined share in work reintegration or currently working
outputs.interpretation: This sums the reintegration and currently-working shares to show the proportion of the cohort retaining some occupational engagement rather than being fully on sick leave; a higher value means more of the cohort kept some work activity despite severe PCC symptoms.

outputs.label: Objective CPET disability rate minus sick-leave rate (positive = more patients meet the objective disability threshold than are formally on sick leave; negative = more patients are on sick leave than meet the objective threshold)
outputs.interpretation: At the document's own baseline values (66.3% objective disability vs. 75% on sick leave), this is negative (about -8.7 percentage points), meaning slightly more patients were on sick leave than strictly met the objective CPET disability threshold in this cohort; it illustrates that formal work status and objective exercise-capacity testing do not map one-to-one here.

outputs.label: Multimorbidity share, ME/CFS-positive minus non-ME/CFS patients (positive = ME/CFS group had a higher multimorbidity share; negative = lower)
outputs.interpretation: At the document's own baseline values (67% vs. 45%), this gap is positive (about 22 percentage points), but the study itself reports this comparison did not reach statistical significance (p=0.056 against its own p<0.05 threshold) and describes it only as 'a trend'; this output should not be read as a confirmed difference between the two groups.

scenarios.label: Pooled multimorbidity (no significant gap)
scenarios.goal: Tests whether the 67%-vs-45% multimorbidity gap survives the study's own non-significant test (p=0.056).
scenarios.description: Sets both ME/CFS-positive and non-ME/CFS multimorbidity rates to the cohort's pooled ~55% rate, reflecting the study's finding that the subgroup difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.056).

scenarios.label: Sick leave matched to CPET threshold
scenarios.goal: Tests whether sick-leave recognition matches objective CPET disability criteria.
scenarios.description: Sets the sick-leave rate equal to the objective CPET-based work disability rate (66.3%), closing the administrative gap the study highlights between subjective sick-leave determination and objective functional testing, illustrative only with no causal mechanism implied.
